title: Autonomy

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Autonomy comes from Greek roots meaning 'self' and 'rule' — you are the one who governs you. Two things have to be true for it to be real: you have to know what your options actually are, and the final call has to be yours. A clinician can describe every door in the house and say which one they would walk through, but they cannot take the key. Fairness, doing good, and keeping promises are all genuine obligations too — they just have their own names and their own logic.

### Question 2

Suppose a friend orders soup and you tell the server, 'No, bring her the salad,' because you think salad is better for her. You may even be right about the nutrition — but the order was hers to place, and you took it. That move has a name: paternalism, from the Latin for 'father,' as though the other adult were a child. The autonomy-respecting version is identical except for one step: you say why you would order the salad, and then you let her order.

### Question 3

A rule shows whether it exists only when someone tests it. If a sign says 'you may leave whenever you like' but the door opens only when staff approve, the sign is decoration. Autonomy becomes visible at the moment a patient says 'no, thank you' and the whole room disagrees — and the answer still stands. Privacy and honesty are real protections too, but they are different promises: one is about who hears your information, the other about what you are told.

### Question 4

Compare holding a driver's license with being fit to drive this car on this road right now. The license is an official status the state grants or revokes — that is competence, and only a court touches it. Whether you can safely handle the vehicle at this moment is something a person evaluates on the spot — that is capacity. A patient can lack capacity for a complex surgical decision at 3 a.m. after sedating medication and clearly have it back by morning, with the 'license' never in question.

### Question 5

Imagine a friend steps out and leaves you to place her order. You do not order what you like, and you do not poll the table — you order what she would have ordered, because you remember she cannot stand olives. That is substituted judgment: the surrogate acts as a messenger for a voice that is temporarily missing, not as a replacement for it. Only when no one has any idea what she would want do you fall back on what is generally good for someone in her situation.

### Question 6

The freedom to swing your arm is real, and it ends where someone else's face begins. A capable adult may accept risk to their own body, and disapproval from family or staff does not shrink that freedom. When a choice can transmit serious illness to strangers who never agreed to the risk, the decision has stopped being self-regarding, and public health authority can set limits — but only the narrowest limit that actually works. The dividing line is other people, not other opinions.

### Question 7

Autonomy means you choose — and one of the things you get to choose is who else sits at the table. A patient who brings her son to every serious conversation because that is how her family works has not given anything up; she has used her authority to set up the process. The mistake to avoid is deciding someone cannot decide just because they want company. Wanting counsel and lacking capacity look nothing alike once you actually check whether the person understands the situation, appreciates how it applies to them, can reason about the options, and can say what they want.

### Question 8

Supporting a choice is like being a good map, not a leash. A complete map shows every road and marks honestly which ones have potholes, then lets the driver pick the route. Nagging until they turn, handing the wheel to their child, or quietly erasing a road from the map all end with someone else driving — and the erased road is the sneakiest, because the driver never knows a choice was taken. The nurse's job is to make the map complete and understood, then stay in the car even if the driver picks the bumpy road.

### Question 9

Capacity is not one master switch that is either on or off; it is a row of switches, one per decision. This man can still reach the switch labeled 'which of my daily pills do I want,' because he understands those and can explain his reasoning. The switch labeled 'major surgery' is out of reach today, so someone helps with that one only. Taking his hand off every switch because one is stuck is not protection — it is a larger loss than the situation calls for.

### Question 10

This law protects a choice in both directions at once: the hospital must tell you the option exists, and it is forbidden from penalizing you for saying 'not now.' Declining the paperwork is itself an answer, and the chart simply records that answer. What the facility cannot do is treat the blank line as a reason to withhold care or as a signal to hand your decisions to a relative — you still have capacity, so you are still the one deciding, form or no form.

### Question 11

There is a real difference between 'no one can make me' and 'I can make you.' Autonomy is the first kind of claim: nothing goes into your body without your agreement. It is not a vending machine in which every button pressed must be dispensed, because the clinician's professional judgment is part of the transaction rather than an obstacle to it. Saying 'we won't do that, here is why, and here is what we can do' does not overrule the patient's choice — it describes what was on offer to choose from.

### Question 12

'That is your call' and 'then I am done with you' are not the same sentence, though they are easy to blur in practice. Think of a coach whose athlete refuses one drill: the coach stops pushing, keeps working with her on everything else, and stays on the deck. Backing off the pressure while staying present is what accepting a refusal looks like. Quietly reducing contact reads as punishment even when it is meant as respect — and the patient still needs the care they never declined.
